description: The European Union grew out of one practical idea: make war between France and Germany physically impossible by tying together coal and steel. Small steps led from **1950** to Maastricht.

hero.hook: Making war impossible by sharing coal and steel.

blocks.text: The **European Union** was not born in one great constitutional night. It moved forward by “small steps.” In the rubble of 1945 the aim was precise: make another war between France and Germany not only unthinkable, but physically impossible.

From the industrial solidarity of **1950** to the political and monetary union of **1992**, Europe invented an integration unlike any other in the world. [[Franco-German reconciliation]] became its engine.

After the war, control of the Ruhr, the great German industrial basin, was the sorest point of all. **Jean Monnet**, a senior French civil servant, and **Robert Schuman**, the foreign minister, put forward a simple idea. On **May 9, 1950**, in the [[Schuman Declaration]], they proposed placing French and German production of coal and steel under a common [[High Authority]].

blocks.caption: Jean Monnet and Robert Schuman, architects of Europe's first steps

blocks.text: Schuman kept the plan so secret that his own diplomats found out only on the morning of the announcement.

Coal and steel are the nerves of any arms industry. In **1951**, the **ECSC** was born, the European Coal and Steel Community. Italy and the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg) joined. For the first time, states handed a slice of sovereignty to a body above them.

On **March 25, 1957**, the Six signed the treaties in Rome that created the **EEC**, the European Economic Community, and **Euratom** for civil nuclear power. The goal was a [[common market]] with no customs barriers, built on the [[four freedoms of the single market]] (goods, people, services, capital).

blocks.caption: Signing the Treaties of Rome, March 25, 1957

blocks.text: In Rome the official treaties were not ready in time. For the photograph, the leaders signed blank pages.

In **1962**, the [[CAP]], the Common Agricultural Policy, reorganized farming. In **1973**, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Denmark joined the club. From a small industrial circle, the EEC grew into a trading power facing the United States and the USSR.

After 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall, integration sped up in order to anchor a reunified Germany. [[The Maastricht Treaty (1992)]] turned the EEC into the **European Union**: European citizenship, a common foreign policy, and economic and monetary union.

blocks.caption: Franco-German reconciliation, the lasting engine of Europe

blocks.text: The **euro** became real on paper in 1999, then as notes and coins on **January 1, 2002**. The single market finally had a single currency. But states also had to accept common budget discipline, a source of future friction.

In the 2000s the EU took in the former Eastern bloc countries, reaching 28 members in 2013. The Treaty of Lisbon reformed the institutions. Then came the shock: **Brexit** (the vote in 2016, departure in 2020). The EU remains a hybrid, more than an organization and less than a state.
